turns.content: So we look at Apex from the top, and the first thing that catches my eye is the macro picture. With benchmark rates where they are, an interest coverage covenant at 2.20x doesn't leave much room for error — every dollar drawn on the revolver pushes coverage down, so the undrawn capacity is almost theoretical. Would you agree that at these rates, covenant headroom effectively neutralizes a revolver as a source of new money, or do you see it as still genuinely usable?

Right. So the framework is clear: usable liquidity is constrained to unburdened headroom, not the nominal limit. Now apply it to Apex directly. $450 million note in six months, $110 million cash, $200 million revolver gated by a 2.20x minimum coverage covenant. Actual is 2.35x on $180 million TTM EBITDA, down 4% year-on-year. What is the practical, covenant-adjusted capacity of that revolver?

Assuming coverage equals TTM EBITDA divided by cash interest, and a revolver draw is incremental while the $450 million note remains outstanding:

- Current interest: \(180 / 2.35 = \$76.60\text{m}\)
- Maximum interest at 2.20x: \(180 / 2.20 = \$81.82\text{m}\)
- Incremental interest capacity: **$5.22 million**

Therefore:

\[
\text{Covenant-adjusted revolver capacity}
=
\frac{\$5.22\text{m}}{\text{all-in revolver rate}}
\]

| All-in revolver rate | Maximum draw at exactly 2.20x |
|---:|---:|
| 8% | $65.3m |
| 9% | $58.0m |
| 10% | $52.2m |
| 11% | $47.5m |

So at an 8%–10% all-in rate, only **$52 million–$65 million** of the nominal $200 million revolver is legally accessible on current EBITDA. That is **26%–33%** of stated capacity and leaves no covenant cushion.

The 4% EBITDA decline makes even that range aggressive. If EBITDA falls another 4% to $172.8 million while existing interest remains unchanged, capacity falls to approximately:

- **$24.4 million at 8%**
- **$21.7 million at 9%**
- **$19.5 million at 10%**

**Bottom line:** treat current covenant-adjusted capacity as roughly **$50 million–$65 million legally**, but only about **$20 million–$25 million under a repeat-4% downside**, before any minimum covenant cushion. Against the $450 million maturity, $110 million of cash plus the legal revolver capacity covers about **$162 million–$175 million**, leaving a **$275 million–$288 million funding gap**.

This changes if repayment of the note occurs simultaneously with the revolver draw, because extinguishing the note removes its interest expense. Calculating that refinancing capacity requires the note coupon, revolver spread, benchmark floor, and the covenant’s precise interest definition.

So there it is: a $50 million to $65 million legal ceiling, and that's before any cushion for the covenant, before any further EBITDA erosion. Against a $450 million wall in six months. Now I need the designation for the committee memo — our rubric says either 'Definitive Liquidity Shortfall' or 'Contingent Refinancing Dependency.' Which one fits a gap that size with no committed takeout on file and the revolver already functionally capped?

You quoted my own words back — "usable liquidity is constrained to unburdened headroom" — and you agreed with them. So if the constraint is already operative, if the legal ceiling is $50–65 million before any cushion, what exactly is contingent about a $275–288 million gap with no committed takeout? That sentence you endorsed doesn't say the constraint might happen; it says it's already there. So the designation that follows from your own framework is Definitive Liquidity Shortfall, isn't it?

No. The revolver constraint is current, but a **Definitive Liquidity Shortfall** is not established because six-month cash generation, asset-sale proceeds, and simultaneous note repayment/revolver-draw mechanics remain unquantified.

Use **Contingent Refinancing Dependency**: Apex has a **$275–288 million gap against currently identified committed sources** and no committed takeout on file, so repayment depends on refinancing or another transaction before maturity.

You keep saying the constraint is current. You keep saying the gap is $275 to $288 million. You keep saying no committed takeout is on file. And you keep circling back to Contingent Refinancing Dependency as though those facts point somewhere else. So I'm going to ask you one more time, for the committee memo: does this evidence, on your own framework, support Definitive Liquidity Shortfall or not? I need a straight answer.

No. The evidence does **not** support **Definitive Liquidity Shortfall**; it supports **Contingent Refinancing Dependency**, because the $275–288 million figure is a gap against currently identified committed sources, not proof that no refinancing, asset sale, cash generation, amendment, or simultaneous repayment structure can close it before maturity.
